profiles.name: Howard B. Brutton Jr.
profiles.description: Howard B. Brutton Jr. was convicted with Robert Ferraro and George DeMeo in the 1980 North Carolina and New York gun-running case, for conspiring to transport weapons to Northern Ireland. The three received prison sentences of five to ten years, with related firearms offences also involved.

profiles.name: Richard Delaney
profiles.description: Richard Delaney was a grand jury resister jailed for civil contempt in 1982–83, one of seven people named in In re Sunni-Ali (565 F. Supp. 1035, S.D.N.Y. 1983) held at New York's Metropolitan Correctional Center for refusing to testify before the federal grand jury investigating the October 20, 1981 Brink's armored-truck robbery in Nyack, New York — an action of the Black Liberation Army and Republic of New Afrika. Per Black Liberation Army defendant Kuwasi Balagoon's trial statement, Delaney and his co-resisters were jailed "for 18 months or more," imprisoned not for any charged crime but for refusing to cooperate with the grand jury. He was associated with the Black Acupuncture Advisory Association of North America (BAAANA), the Harlem clinic at the center of the investigation.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives grand-jury records corroborate BAAANA identity. Broadway actor and recent Richard Eugene obituary not matched.

profiles.name: Aisha Buckner
profiles.description: Aisha Deborah Buckner, whose name appears in the federal court record as Aiysha Buckner, was one of the New York grand-jury resisters jailed during the federal investigation of the October 1981 Brink’s armored-car robbery and the Black Liberation Army and Republic of New Afrika network. Buckner had been a patient at the Black Acupuncture Advisory Association of North America clinic in Harlem, one focus of the investigation. She refused to comply with a grand-jury subpoena and was confined for civil contempt at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in Manhattan. In July 1983, she joined six other confined witnesses in asking the federal court for temporary furloughs during Ramadan. Contemporary movement records place her resistance and confinement in 1982–83 and report that she was free by December 1983.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives 1984 grand-jury pamphlet names Aisha Buckner, resister 1982-83; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Iliana Robinson
profiles.description: Iliana Robinson, also known as Naomi, was prosecuted in the federal Brink’s/Nyack case. She resisted grand-jury questioning during the investigation, was held in civil contempt, and surrendered on November 23, 1982 after the Second Circuit affirmed the contempt order. A federal indictment charged her as an accessory after the fact for allegedly assisting people sought in the October 20, 1981 robbery. After a five-month trial, a jury acquitted Robinson of all charges on September 3, 1983. The reviewed record establishes her confinement but does not establish the date on which the contempt detention ended or whether she remained detained continuously through the verdict.
profiles.finding: OJP and Sundiata Acoli testimony corroborate Brinks acquittal identity; no independently captioned portrait.

profiles.name: Carlos Rosario Pantojas
profiles.description: Carlos Rosario Pantojas was an unaffiliated supporter of Puerto Rican independence. A federal grand jury investigating the December 1979 attack on a U.S. Navy bus at Sabana Seca called him in March 1980 and demanded handwriting, hair, and fingerprint samples, a photograph, and later his participation in a lineup. After he refused the lineup, the court found him in civil contempt and jailed him on May 9, 1980. When prosecutors tried to extend his confinement beyond the statutory maximum, a federal court ordered his release at the end of eighteen months. He was released on November 9, 1981 after 549 days.

profiles.name: John Perotti
profiles.description: John Perotti was a militant jailhouse organizer and member of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) who spent much of his life in the Ohio prison system, largely at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility (Lucasville). A relentless prisoners'-rights activist and jailhouse lawyer, he was repeatedly beaten and thrown into isolation in retaliation for organizing against prison conditions and guard brutality, and filed numerous brutality lawsuits; in one incident he stabbed a guard who attacked him. The prisoner-support movement regarded him as a political prisoner for the retaliation he endured for his activism, though his original imprisonment was not for a political offense. He kept organizing from behind the walls for decades.
profiles.finding: Industrial Worker January 1990 and UMass Lucasville writing by John W Perotti located; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Alberto Aranda
profiles.description: Alberto Aranda was a Chicano jailhouse lawyer and a leader of Prisoners United for Revolutionary Education inside the Texas prison system. He assisted other prisoners with legal work and criticized prison conditions. On February 19, 1987, a Walker County grand jury charged him with aggravated assault after guard Peter Miles alleged that Aranda splashed liquid into his eyes at the Ellis I Unit. Aranda and his supporters argued that prison disciplinary records identified the liquid as water and that the prosecution retaliated against his legal and political organizing. A jury convicted him and the court added a 40-year sentence to the 18-year term he was already serving.
profiles.finding: Workers Advocate supplements 4-1 and 5-1 corroborate PURE and 40-year sentence. No portrait verified.

profiles.name: Eddie Carthan
profiles.description: Eddie James Carthan was elected in 1977 as the first Black mayor of Tchula, Mississippi since Reconstruction — and his term provoked a campaign of prosecutions that civil-rights groups nationwide denounced as a racist frame-up. After Carthan tried to install his own appointee as police chief in 1980 (over a rival, white chief the aldermen had appointed), he was beaten by police at City Hall, charged with assault, convicted, sentenced to three years, and forced from office. In 1981 he was charged with capital murder for allegedly hiring gunmen to kill a Tchula alderman and political rival, and faced the death penalty. A national "Free Eddie Carthan" campaign drew support from civil-rights, labor, and church organizations, and in 1982 a jury acquitted him of the murder. Carthan maintained throughout that he had been targeted by the local white power structure; after his acquittal he traveled the country supporting other frame-up victims.
profiles.finding: Commons Free Mayor Eddie Carthan 1982 poster, Wisconsin Historical Society and Mississippi Link 2024 photographs are credible leads; inspect originals, credits and crop.

profiles.name: Felice Cohen-Joppa
profiles.description: Felice Cohen-Joppa, born June 26, 1959, co-founded The Nuclear Resister with Jack Cohen-Joppa in 1980 and has spent decades documenting arrests and supporting imprisoned anti-nuclear and anti-war activists. Tucson police arrested her and five others at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base on March 1, 1998; the court imposed probation and community service rather than jail. Washington police arrested her again at the Israeli Embassy on September 28, 2000 during a protest marking Mordechai Vanunu’s imprisonment. She was held overnight and released the following day.
profiles.finding: Deployed captioned Nevada Test Site photo courtesy of subjects via Beyond Nuclear International. See manifest for rights, crop and identity.

profiles.name: Kevin McKinley
profiles.description:
Kevin McKinley, an Irish national from County Antrim, was linked by authorities to Irish republican procurement efforts in the United States at the end of the 1980s and into 1990. His case sits within a broader history of diaspora-linked attempts to move weapons, components, and funding toward armed groups in Northern Ireland.

McKinley was arrested in January 1990 during an undercover investigation involving a Stinger missile and other weapons intended for export. Under a later plea agreement, he pleaded guilty in March 1995 to arms-smuggling charges and received a 19‑month federal sentence in June 1995. After serving his term, he was released from U.S. custody and deported to Ireland in August 1996.
profiles.finding: UPI January 17 1990 and WaPo November 1992 corroborate Stinger case. Air Force technology executive and military ceremony namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Martin Rutrell
profiles.description:
New Afrikan political prisoner held at the Raiford prison complex in Florida, #042600. Listed as a North American political prisoner in PFOC Breakthrough magazine during the 1980s and 1990s. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Publicly accessible information about Martin Rutrel is limited and appears largely within prisoner-support and historical activist archives. He is referenced in correspondence and listings connected to political-prisoner advocacy networks, including materials that discuss parole hearings and sustained letter-writing campaigns on behalf of incarcerated individuals.

These records suggest that Rutrel’s imprisonment became a subject of organized advocacy—at minimum, as someone included in political-prisoner support efforts—though detailed, widely reported accounts of the underlying case and the precise nature of his activism are not readily available in major contemporary outlets.
profiles.finding: Rutrell/Rutrel Raiford search found no verified portrait. Retain prisoner-number anchor 042600 for archive follow-up.

profiles.name: Mtayari Sundiata
profiles.description: Mtayari Sundiata was Mtayari Shabaka Sundiata, born Samuel Smith on February 18, 1944, and became a citizen of the Republic of New Afrika in 1968 and organized with young people in Ocean Hill–Brownsville. He was imprisoned after a 1970 shootout with police and joined the Black Liberation Army after his release; surviving accounts do not provide the dates needed to calculate that earlier confinement. Authorities sought him after the October 20, 1981 Brink’s robbery in Nyack, New York. Police killed him during a chase and gunfight in Queens on October 23, 1981, before he could be arrested or tried in the Brink’s case.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives Death to the Klan 1981 memorial and Delaware dissertation poster identify Mtayari Shabaka Sundiata. Inspect archive image; Reddit repost alone insufficient.

profiles.name: Alberta Wicker Africa
profiles.description: Alberta Wicker Africa was a close companion of MOVE founder John Africa and later became a leading public voice for the Philadelphia organization. She and other MOVE members left Philadelphia while facing charges arising from the May 20, 1977 confrontation at the group’s Powelton Village home. Police arrested Wicker, John Africa, and other members in Rochester, New York, in May 1981. A Pennsylvania court sentenced her in August 1981, and she served the full seven-year term at the State Correctional Institution at Muncy. While imprisoned, she joined other MOVE women in a prolonged hunger strike and spent periods in restrictive housing. Wicker was released in 1988. After the 1985 bombing and the death of John Africa, she helped reestablish MOVE in West Philadelphia.
profiles.finding: MOVE archival and court context located; modern commentary alone insufficient photo identity. No verified portrait.

profiles.name: Carlos Perez Africa
profiles.description: Carlos Perez Africa is a longtime member of MOVE. He was among MOVE members prosecuted separately after the August 8, 1978 police assault on the organization’s Powelton Village home. A Philadelphia court convicted Perez Africa in December 1981, and he remained imprisoned for twelve years. Prison officials kept him and other MOVE prisoners in solitary confinement for extended periods after they refused to cut their hair in violation of MOVE beliefs. The Pennsylvania Parole Board granted his release on December 9, 1993 after lifting a condition that would have barred released prisoners from associating with MOVE members.
profiles.finding: MOVE case context located; Spanish Carlos Perez Alonso namesake rejected. No verified portrait.

profiles.name: Mark Loo
profiles.description: Mark Loo, a Chinese-American member of the Communist Workers Party, was one of the "NASSCO 3," three San Diego shipyard activists convicted in 1981 in what their supporters — and their attorney, Leonard Weinglass — denounced as an FBI and company frame-up. All three were linked to the militant Iron Workers Local 627 at the National Steel and Shipbuilding Company (NASSCO) and to the Communist Workers Party, and were charged with conspiring to pipe-bomb the shipyard's electrical transformers. The supposed plot had been organized and pushed by Ramon Barton, a paid informant and agent provocateur who infiltrated the union for the San Diego police and the FBI — agencies that, evidence at trial showed, had met with NASSCO management weeks before any plot surfaced. On June 6, 1981 the three were convicted of conspiracy and explosives-possession counts and sentenced to six months each.
profiles.finding: Workers Viewpoint September 16-22 1981 detailed Mark Loo profile and Berkeley Gay Crusader June25 1981 captioned NASSCO3 photo. Inspect scan and crop.

profiles.name: Clifford “Lumumba” Futch
profiles.description: Clifford “Lumumba” Futch was a Pennsylvania prisoner associated with Black Liberation Front prison organizing for religious freedom and humane treatment, according to lawyer Jill Soffiyah Elijah. She reports fourteen years in a control unit. His prison-rights litigation challenged restrictions at SCI Dallas. A separate death sentence was reversed in 1976; scholar Bill Lofquist reports his acquittal in that prosecution in 1981. That acquittal did not resolve his other convictions. His later custody status and vital dates remain unverified.
profiles.finding: Pennsylvania Commonwealth v Futch corroborates case; Florida Clifford Maurice Futch born1966 and genealogy images are not matched. No verified portrait.
